newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, at Iowa picnic, serves up bit of red meat.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, at Iowa picnic, serves up bit of red meat.

text.p: President Bill Clinton ate no red meat at Sen. Tom Harkin's annual "Steak n' Chop Fry" on Sunday but he served up a little, blaming the Republicans for three government shutdowns.

In a quick, four-hour campaign visit to a farm state that holds just seven electoral college votes, Clinton was out to support fellow Democrats in their congressional races as he worked to hold on to the presidency.
Wearing cowboy boots, khaki pants and an open-necked blue shirt, Clinton stood on a stage built from bales of hay and and took on Republicans who control Congress.
"We clearly had the ability to balance the budget in the last two years and they said: we're going to shut the government down if you don't do it our way," Clinton said.

"(They said) We're going to give you a tax cut, Mr. President, and the people in your income group whether you want it or not, and we're going to cut Medicare, we're going to walk away from the guarantee Medicaid has given for 30 years," he added.

"That's our balanced budget plan, if you don't like it, we're going to shut the government down. And I said, the Democratic party does not love the government, it loves the people -- shut her down," Clinton said to loud cheers.

Organisers had said they expected 10,000-12,000 people at the picnic -- a $15 per person carniverous celebration. The turnout at Harkin's 19th annual event, however, appeared far lower on an unseasonably cool day with the smell of grilled beef and pork heavy in the air.

The money raised on Sunday -- estimated at $400,000 over three events -- will be split between Harkin, who is seeking a third term, and the Democratic party's effort to elect its candidates in local and state elections.
Leading Republican Bob Dole by 15 to 20 points in national polls, Clinton tried to nail down Iowa, which voted for him in 1992 and for losing Democrat Michael Dukakis in 1988.
Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart told reporters that a Mason-Dixon poll taken Sept. 8-10 gave Clinton a 10 point lead in the state.
But from a congressional point of view, Iowa is a different story, with Harkin the only Democrat among the state's two senators and five members of the House of Representatives.
"It's a state where we hope to pick up some congressional seats -- and we're not going to take it for granted (in the presidential race)," White House political director Doug Sosnik told Reuters.

Campaign officials say that at this stage of the game, with the first Clinton-Dole debate scheduled for Sept. 26, they are particularly concerned about making sure their candidate remains well-rested.

Clinton, who returned on Friday from a grueling three-day campaign trip to four western states, made a brief visit to North Carolina on Saturday to inspect hurricane damage and was to make a one-day visit to Ohio on Monday.
On his way back from North Carolina, Clinton joked that the one-day trips were a welcome relief, telling reporters: "We'll have to have more of this. I am getting old and tired."
Clinton sets off on a four-day campaign swing on Tuesday that will take him to Michigan, Illinois, Arizona, Washington and Oregon.
